title: HTTP Caching: Cache-Control, Validators and CDNs
summary: A practical guide to how HTTP caching works: Cache-Control directives, ETag/Last-Modified validation with 304 responses, the Vary header, browser vs CDN vs proxy caches, hashed-filename cache busting, and the misconfigurations that bite in production.

chapters.title: Why HTTP Caching Matters
points: Caching stores a copy of a response so a later request can reuse it instead of hitting the origin
Three wins: lower latency, less bandwidth, less origin load
Cache hit vs cache miss: a hit is served from the cache, a miss goes to the origin and may store the result
Freshness: a stored response is fresh while its age is below its freshness lifetime
Staleness: a stale response must be revalidated (or served under explicit stale rules) before reuse
Only cacheable methods and status codes are stored by default: GET/HEAD with 200, 301, 404 etc.; POST is rarely cached
Heuristic freshness: with no explicit lifetime, caches may guess ~10% of (Date - Last-Modified)
Age header: how many seconds a response has sat in shared caches
Request flow: browser cache -> CDN edge -> proxy/origin shield -> origin
Shared cache (CDN, proxy) serves many users; private cache (browser) serves one

chapters.title: Cache-Control Basics: max-age and s-maxage
points: Cache-Control is the modern header that governs caching; it overrides Expires and Pragma
Syntax: comma-separated directives, e.g. Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600
max-age=N: response is fresh for N seconds after it was generated, counted from the Date header
s-maxage=N: same as max-age but applies only to shared caches and overrides max-age there
Example: Cache-Control: max-age=60, s-maxage=3600 gives browsers 1 minute and CDNs 1 hour
Expires: legacy absolute date; ignored if max-age is present
max-age=0 means immediately stale, so every use requires revalidation
Time is relative to response generation, not receipt, so Age header is subtracted from lifetime
Request-side Cache-Control (e.g. max-age=0, no-cache on reload) lets clients demand fresh copies
s-maxage also implies the response is allowed in shared caches even if it carries Authorization
Pragma: no-cache is an HTTP/1.0 request relic and not reliable as a response header

chapters.title: no-cache vs no-store
points: no-cache does NOT mean don't cache: the response may be stored but must be revalidated before every reuse
no-store means never write the response to any cache, browser or shared
no-cache gives you caching plus freshness guarantee; no-store gives you no caching at all
Use no-store for sensitive data: banking pages, tokens, personal data
Use no-cache for HTML shells that should always be checked but can still get a cheap 304
Comparison table: no-cache = stored + revalidate; no-store = not stored; max-age=0 = stored + stale immediately
must-revalidate: once stale, the cache must not serve it without successful revalidation, even if the origin is down
no-cache, no-store together is redundant; no-store alone is enough
Mistake: using no-cache to mean no-store for private data, leaving a copy on disk
Even no-store cannot protect data from the user's own browser history/back-button in all cases; test it
Back/forward cache (bfcache) can restore pages regardless of caching headers unless no-store is set

chapters.title: public, private, immutable, stale-while-revalidate
points: public: any cache, including shared ones, may store the response, even if it looks personalized or has Authorization
private: only the end user's browser cache may store it; CDNs and proxies must not
Default for responses with Authorization is not shared-cacheable unless public, s-maxage or must-revalidate is set
immutable: tells the browser the body will never change during its freshness lifetime, so skip revalidation even on reload
immutable matters because reloading normally triggers conditional requests for every asset
Example for fingerprinted assets: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
stale-while-revalidate=N: serve the stale copy instantly for up to N seconds while refreshing in the background
Example: Cache-Control: max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300 hides revalidation latency from users
stale-if-error=N: serve stale for N seconds if the origin returns 5xx or is unreachable
SWR trade-off: users may see content up to max-age + N seconds old, so pick N by how stale is acceptable
Browser support for immutable varies (Safari/Firefox yes; others ignore safely since it's an optimization)
Per-directive scope: s-maxage and public target shared caches; private and immutable target the browser

chapters.title: Validators: ETag and Last-Modified
points: Validators let a cache ask 'has this changed?' cheaply instead of re-downloading
Last-Modified: timestamp of last change, one-second resolution, sent as an HTTP date
ETag: opaque identifier of a specific representation version, e.g. ETag: "a1b2c3"
Strong ETag "abc" means byte-for-byte identical; weak ETag W/"abc" means semantically equivalent
ETag generation: content hash (MD5/SHA), version number, or inode+size+mtime
ETag beats Last-Modified: it handles sub-second changes, reverts, and non-file content
If both are present, caches use both; ETag takes precedence for If-None-Match matching
Gotcha: per-server ETags (inode-based) differ across load-balanced nodes, causing needless 200s
Gotcha: compression middleware can alter or strip the ETag; gzip vs br variants need distinct ETags
Range requests require strong validators; weak ETags cannot be used with If-Range
Last-Modified in the future or constantly updating (dynamic pages) breaks heuristic freshness
Without any validator, a stale response can only be re-fetched in full

chapters.title: Conditional Requests and 304 Not Modified
points: Flow: client sends validator back; origin compares and replies 304 with no body or 200 with fresh body
If-None-Match: "a1b2c3" pairs with ETag; server returns 304 if any listed tag matches
If-Modified-Since: <date> pairs with Last-Modified; 304 if resource not modified after that date
If-None-Match takes precedence when both conditions are sent
Example exchange: GET /app.css -> 200 + ETag "v7"; later GET with If-None-Match: "v7" -> 304 Not Modified
A 304 has no body but should repeat Cache-Control, Expires, ETag, Vary so the cache can update freshness
After a 304 the cache resets the freshness clock and serves its stored body
Cost of a 304: one round trip with tiny headers, saving bandwidth but not latency
If-Match and If-Unmodified-Since are for writes (optimistic concurrency), returning 412 Precondition Failed
If-Range: resume a partial download only if the validator still matches, else send the full body
Mistake: server ignores If-None-Match and always returns 200, wasting bandwidth
Mistake: returning 304 without a matching Vary-aware check, serving wrong variant
Browser reload sends max-age=0 conditional requests; hard reload (Ctrl+Shift+R) bypasses caches entirely

chapters.title: The Vary Header
points: Vary lists request headers that influenced the response; caches key stored copies on URL plus those header values
Example: Vary: Accept-Encoding stores separate gzip and brotli copies of the same URL
Vary: Accept-Language for localized content; Vary: Accept for content negotiation (e.g. WebP vs JPEG)
Vary: Cookie makes each cookie value a separate entry, which kills CDN hit rate
Vary: * means the response is never reusable by shared caches without revalidating
Vary: User-Agent fragments the cache into thousands of variants; normalize at the CDN instead
Missing Vary is a correctness bug: a gzip body may be served to a client that cannot decode it
Mistake: personalised content on a public URL without Vary or private leaks one user's page to others
CDNs let you normalize or whitelist headers in the cache key to limit variants
Vary applies to revalidation too: a 304 must correspond to the same variant
Prefer separate URLs for variants (/en/, /fr/) over Vary when you can: simpler and more cache-friendly

chapters.title: Browser vs CDN vs Proxy Caches
points: Browser cache: private, per user and per device, honors private and no-store; fastest, zero network
CDN edge: shared across all users in a region, honors s-maxage and public, offloads the origin
Forward proxy: sits in front of clients (corporate/ISP) and shares responses among that group
Reverse proxy (Varnish, nginx, Cloudflare): sits in front of origin servers, caches for all clients
Layered lookup: browser -> CDN edge -> regional/shield tier -> origin, each with its own TTL
Comparison table columns: scope, who controls it, purge ability, honors private, typical TTL
You cannot purge a browser cache remotely; you can purge CDN caches via API, tag, or URL
CDN-Cache-Control, Surrogate-Control and Cloudflare-CDN-Cache-Control let you give the CDN a different policy than browsers
Example split: Cache-Control: max-age=0 for browsers with CDN-Cache-Control: max-age=86400 and purge on deploy
Cache status headers: X-Cache: HIT/MISS, CF-Cache-Status, Age, and the standard Cache-Status
CDNs may ignore origin headers by default for some extensions or add their own minimum TTLs
Caching of redirects (301 is cached long, 302 per headers) can trap users on old targets

chapters.title: Cache Busting with Hashed Filenames
points: Problem: long TTLs make updates invisible until expiry, and you cannot purge browsers
Solution: put a content hash in the filename so a new build means a new URL, e.g. app.3f9a1c.js
Assets get Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable since the URL changes when content does
HTML entry point references the hashed names and gets no-cache or a short TTL
Bundlers produce hashes automatically: webpack [contenthash], Vite and Rollup [hash], Next.js _next/static
Query-string busting (app.js?v=2) works for browsers but some proxies and CDNs ignore query strings in cache keys
Content hash beats build timestamp or version number: unchanged files keep their URL and stay cached
Deploy order: upload new hashed assets first, then publish the new HTML, so no page references a missing file
Keep the previous build's assets for a while so users with old HTML do not get 404s
Mistake: hashed asset served with short TTL wastes the benefit; non-hashed asset with long TTL traps users on old files
Cascading hashes: if a shared chunk changes, every file that imports it changes hash; split vendor code to limit this
Service worker files and manifest.json should not be hash-cached long, or updates never arrive

chapters.title: Common Misconfigurations and Cheatsheet
points: Mistake: HTML cached with long max-age, so users stay on old releases until expiry
Mistake: no-cache confused with no-store, leaking sensitive data into caches
Mistake: Set-Cookie on cacheable responses; many CDNs refuse to cache them or cache one user's session
Mistake: missing Vary: Accept-Encoding or an overly broad Vary: Cookie/User-Agent
Mistake: relying only on Last-Modified with load-balanced servers whose file times differ
Mistake: assuming a CDN purge clears browser caches; it does not
Mistake: Expires and max-age disagreeing, since max-age wins but confuses debugging
Mistake: caching error responses (5xx, soft 404s) with the same long TTL as success
Debug: curl -I, DevTools Network tab (from memory/disk cache), Age and X-Cache headers
Cheatsheet: HTML = no-cache + ETag; hashed assets = public, max-age=31536000, immutable; API user data = private, no-store; public API = s-maxage + stale-while-revalidate
Cheatsheet: sensitive = no-store; revalidate always = no-cache; CDN-only TTL = s-maxage
Summary: cache aggressively with unique URLs, validate cheaply with ETags, and keep personalized data out of shared caches
